record.title: A controlled benchmark reports token-level fixes for language-model data attribution
record.summary: A preprint introduces the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT), which fine-tunes Qwen3.5-4B models on fictitious facts so the training documents provide known attribution ground truth. Across controlled settings, the authors report that redundancy and lexical distractors degrade gradient-based methods, while token-level negative log-odds gradients combined with top-k token aggregation improve fact-tracing recall by 35–72 percentage points. On FTRACE-TREX, the paper reports that negative log-odds improves counterfactual retraining performance for TRAK, EK-FAC and Grad-Dot by up to 4.9×. The tested tasks use single-token predictions and single-task LoRA fine-tuning; transfer to real pretraining attribution, multi-token outputs and multi-task learning remains unestablished.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors published arXiv:2610.40655v1 introducing the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT), code/data availability, controlled task design and evaluation of gradient-based attribution methods.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that redundancy and lexical distractors degrade attribution performance, and that token-level negative log-odds gradients with top-k token aggregation increase ground-truth recall by 35–72 percentage points across tested CATT settings.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On FTRACE-TREX, the authors report that negative log-odds improves counterfactual retraining performance for TRAK, EK-FAC and Grad-Dot, with a maximum reported improvement of 4.9× for TRAK at the largest tested removal budget.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish that the reported improvements transfer to multi-token predictions, multi-task training, realistic large-scale pretraining attribution, copyright adjudication or general model-behavior tracing; the authors identify the first two as limitations.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the CATT or FTRACE-TREX results was inspected, and linked code/data/checkpoints were not audited.
Transfer from single-token, single-task LoRA fact tracing to multi-token behavior, multi-task training and realistic pretraining corpora is unestablished.

brief.importance_rationale: If the token-level attribution improvements replicate on realistic training data and multi-token behaviors, they could change the validity of evidence used in model-data auditing, copyright/credit analysis and behavior tracing. Current support is a preprint's controlled single-token benchmark and one external benchmark; broad transfer is unestablished.
limitations: All quantitative results are first-party preprint reports and have not been independently reproduced in this activation.
The diagnostic CATT task uses fictitious single-token facts, Qwen3.5-4B and single-task LoRA fine-tuning; it does not reproduce realistic pretraining attribution conditions.
The authors state that multi-token prediction and multi-task attribution are not evaluated, and top-k token aggregation introduces a hyperparameter without real-world ground-truth validation signals.
The authors note strong BM25 performance on some synthetic tasks and call for evaluations where surface lexical overlap is not a reliable shortcut.
brief.summary: A preprint introduces the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT), which fine-tunes Qwen3.5-4B models on fictitious facts so the training documents provide known attribution ground truth. Across controlled settings, the authors report that redundancy and lexical distractors degrade gradient-based methods, while token-level negative log-odds gradients combined with top-k token aggregation improve fact-tracing recall by 35–72 percentage points. On FTRACE-TREX, the paper reports that negative log-odds improves counterfactual retraining performance for TRAK, EK-FAC and Grad-Dot by up to 4.9×. The tested tasks use single-token predictions and single-task LoRA fine-tuning; transfer to real pretraining attribution, multi-token outputs and multi-task learning remains unestablished.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report 35–72 percentage-point recall improvements on synthetic controlled fact tracing and up to 4.9× improvement in FTRACE-TREX counterfactual retraining performance for TRAK.
technical.compute_or_cost: The authors report a 2,426 GPU-hour attribution sweep across 843 final-attempt jobs on A100-80GB, H100 and H200 GPUs; there is no dollar, energy or labor estimate. Because hardware allocation across methods was nonrandom, pooled cross-method totals are not like-for-like. In A100-only estimates at 5,000 candidate documents, one EK-FAC job took 39 hours per model, the layerwise-project job 6.6 hours, and dense TRAK 2.7 hours. These are first-party runtime measurements, not independently audited or reproduced.
technical.demonstrated_result: A preprint, benchmark design and experiment results are available for inspection. The numerical efficacy results remain author-reported; no code, data, trained checkpoints or independent reproduction were inspected in this activation.
technical.mechanism: Attribution scores use gradient-based influence estimates, but document averaging can dilute localized evidence. Authors apply negative log-odds gradients at token level to avoid confidence-dependent suppression, then optionally aggregate only top-k token scores within each training document.
technical.regime: CATT uses Qwen3.5-4B models LoRA-fine-tuned on fictitious single-token facts across two task types, with three seeds per configuration. FTRACE-TREX provides an external benchmark using counterfactual retraining; results do not establish transfer to large pretraining corpora or multi-token/multi-task attribution.
technical.reproducibility: The paper says code, data and trained models are available at its project page; this review inspected the arXiv HTML only. No artifacts were downloaded or executed and no independent replication was found in this check.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares standard cross-entropy gradient and document-level aggregation against token-level negative log-odds and top-k aggregation, across gradient similarity, Fisher/influence, GGN-based and training-dynamics methods; BM25 retrieval is a strong lexical baseline on synthetic settings.

brief.title: A controlled benchmark reports token-level fixes for language-model data attribution
brief.why_it_matters: If the reported effects replicate beyond the controlled benchmark, attribution systems used for training-data audits, copyright inquiries and model-behavior tracing may need token-level loss and aggregation choices that preserve localized evidence. This is a paper-reported method result, not proof that existing attribution systems are generally unreliable or that the correction transfers to large-scale pretraining.
